title: Which frying pan? Five kinds, side by side
summary: Cast iron, carbon steel, stainless steel, non-stick and ceramic: what each one does well, and what you give up.
note: The pilot guide, from the frying pan trial in Claude Design

settings.markdown:
No pan is best at everything. A heavy pan holds its heat when cold meat goes in, but is slow to cool down. A coated pan lets an egg slide off, but does not like high heat and wears out. Most kitchens do well with two: one that can take a lot of heat, and one that food does not stick to.

Below are the five common kinds, scored on the same six things, then a quick way to pick one for the job in front of you.

settings.title: Five pans, the same six questions
settings.text: Scores from 1 to 5, compared with each other. More is always better for you as a cook: for easy care, 5 is the least work.

items.name: Cast iron

facts.best: Steak, potatoes, dishes that finish in the oven

items.pick: you sear a lot of meat and want one pan that lasts a lifetime.
items.avoid: you want something light, or wash everything in the dishwasher.

items.name: Carbon steel

facts.best: Stir-fries, steak, eggs once it is well seasoned

items.pick: you want the searing of cast iron with a lighter pan that answers faster.
items.avoid: you cook a lot with tomato, wine or lemon.

items.name: Stainless steel
items.pick: you make pan sauces and want a pan that goes in the dishwasher.
items.avoid: you mostly fry eggs and fish.

items.name: Non-stick
items.pick: breakfast and gentle frying are what you cook most.
items.avoid: you want to fry on full heat, or want to avoid PFAS.

items.name: Ceramic coating
items.pick: you want food to slide off without PTFE, and accept a shorter life.
items.avoid: you expect the coating to last for many years.

settings.note: Non-stick here means a PTFE coating (often sold as Teflon). Ceramic coatings are free of PFAS but lose their non-stick sooner.

settings.title: What are you cooking?
settings.text: Pick the job, and see the pan that does it best and what you give up by choosing it.

tasks.label: Steak and hard searing
tasks.why: The heavy pan holds its heat when cold meat goes in, so the temperature drops little and the crust browns evenly.
tasks.tip: Heat it for 5 to 10 minutes on medium-high before the meat goes in.
tasks.cost: Heavy to lift, and it must be dried and wiped with a little oil after washing.
tasks.alt_why: almost as good a crust, and lighter

tasks.label: Eggs and omelettes
tasks.why: Nothing sticks, even on low heat with a drop of butter, which is just what eggs need.
tasks.tip: Stay on low to medium heat, and use wooden or silicone tools.
tasks.cost: The coating wears and needs replacing after a few years. It does not take high heat.
tasks.alt_why: free of PFAS, but loses its non-stick sooner

tasks.label: Pan sauces and browning
tasks.why: The browned bits left on the bottom are the start of the sauce, and steel takes the acid of wine and tomato without tasting of it.
tasks.tip: Pour in wine or stock while the pan is hot, and scrape the bits loose.
tasks.cost: Food sticks if the pan is not hot enough, or if you turn it too soon.
tasks.alt_why: browns well too, but does not like long cooking with acid

tasks.label: Stir-fries and fast high heat
tasks.why: It answers fast when you turn the heat up or down, takes full heat, and gets slicker the more you use it.
tasks.tip: Season it with a thin layer of oil before the first use, and wash it without soap.
tasks.cost: It rusts if left wet, and acidic dishes discolour it.
tasks.alt_why: takes the heat, but food sticks more easily

tasks.label: Fish with the skin on
tasks.why: The skin lets go without much fat, and the coating is free of PFAS.
tasks.tip: Medium heat. Leave the skin until it lets go by itself.
tasks.cost: It loses its non-stick sooner than the others, especially at high heat.
tasks.alt_why: lets go even more easily, and lasts longer

settings.markdown:
## Looking after them

- **Cast iron and carbon steel:** wash with hot water and a brush, dry on the hob, and wipe with a few drops of oil. A little soap now and then does no harm; the dishwasher does.
- **Stainless steel:** anything goes, dishwasher included. Burnt-on bits come off after a soak, or with a paste of baking soda.
- **Non-stick and ceramic:** no metal tools, no full heat on an empty pan, and wash by hand. When food starts to stick, the coating is worn out.
